legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Scaling Laws for Precision", Tanishq Kumar, Zachary Ankner, Benjamin F. Spector, Blake Bordelon, Niklas Muennighoff, Mansheej Paul, Cengiz Pehlevan, Christopher Ré, Aditi Raghunathan (Harvard, Stanford, MIT, Databricks, CMU). The PDF shows "arXiv:2411.04330v2 [cs.LG] 30 Nov 2024", with no venue printed (I searched for ICLR, no hit). Treat it as an arXiv preprint, 2024. If you cite a conference version, check it elsewhere. I did not read that from this PDF.

COVERAGE: All 100258 chars were extracted and read, about 36 pages. That covers the main text, conclusion and limitations, and Appendices A-O (A-N in text, O is plots). References were skimmed. Figure axes extracted as garbled numbers, so I used captions only. No embedded instructions found.

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. Post-train quantization (PTQ) degradation grows with training tokens, a power law in D/N times an exponential in PTQ bits.
 - number: delta_PTQ(N,D,Ppost) = C_T (D^γD / N^γN) e^(-Ppost/γpost). Fitted: C_T=0.0598, γD=0.5068, γN=0.3439 (Table 2, App K). R2=0.97 over all fitted points.
 - setup: BF16-trained OLMo-style Transformer++ on Dolma V1.7. N = 30, 60, 110, 220M non-embedding params; D = 1.5, 3, 6, 13, 26B tokens; D/N up to about 10^3. PTQ with GPTQ to INT3 to INT6. Replicated with AWQ and round-to-nearest (App F), and with a linear-decay LR schedule at 30M (App G).
 - quote: "We find that the degradation δPTQ increases in training data size across all model sizes, but that for a fixed dataset size larger models incur a smaller degradation. We additionally observe that δPTQ increases exponentially as we decrease the precision we quantize to."
 - where: Sec 3.1, Fig 2, Eq 2, p.4-6.

2. Past a critical data size, more pretraining hurts the quantized model (Finding 1).
 - number: D_crit = (βB N^γN e^(Ppost/γpost) / (γD C_T))^(1/(γD+β)). It explodes in P, so 8-bit needs an unreasonable amount of data. For D/N >> 10^3, effects "become nontrivial around 5-bits, and dominant below that".
 - quote: "This implies that for models that will be post-train quantized, there exists an amount of pretraining data beyond which additional data is actively harmful to performance at inference-time"
 - where: Sec 3.1; App E.1 (p.25).
 - Fig 2 shows loss after PTQ rising with data at small N / low bits. The abstract says the same: "eventually making additional pretraining data actively harmful".

3. Compute-optimal training precision is about 7-8 bits, independent of compute (Finding 3).
 - number: P* ≈ 7-8 bits. 16-bit has "many unnecessary bits". 4-bit forces model size up by "more than 4x".
 - setup: fitted on integer-type quantized training (weights, activations and KV all at P). Cost model C = (6/16)·N·D·P (compute linear in P). Validated by compute-matched FP4 to FP32 runs, 220M to 1.6B params, on Dolma val loss. Fig 6: predicted optimum near 7-8 bits, and integer fit is good until 4-bit.
 - quote: "We find this P* to be around 7-8 bits when fitting our scaling law on runs with quantization done to integer type. This has two consequences: first, this means the de-facto practice of training models in 16-bit may be suboptimal. Second, the race to low-precision training may have to stop before going below 4-bits"
 - where: Sec 4.3.2, p.9-10; Finding 3.
 - Caveat: compute savings are assumed linear in bits, but the authors say real gains are less than 2x due to systems overhead.

4. If model size N is fixed in advance, compute-optimal precision rises with compute.
 - number: P*(C) ∝ log C ≈ log(D/N). At fixed precision P, lowering P at fixed compute means increasing params and decreasing data (Eq 6).
 - quote: "when N is fixed in advance, such as when training a model family on similar data, P*(C) ∝ log C. This suggests that for models that will be significantly overtrained, higher precision during training may be compute-optimal."
 - where: Sec 4.3.3, Finding 3, p.10. Fig 6 right marks Llama-3 8B, 70B, 405B.

5. Effective parameter count: bits and parameters trade off, with saturation around 6-7 bits per weight.
 - number: Neff = N(1−e^(−Pw/γw)), γw=2.6745. Joint form Neff = N(1−e^(−Pw/γw))(1−e^(−Pa/γa))(1−e^(−Pkv/γkv)), with γa (listed "γi") = 2.2102 and γkv = 0.9578. Loss = A·Neff^(−α) + B·D^(−β) + E, with A=4.299e3, α=β=0.4965, B=1.806e4, E=2.7648. Fit R2: 0.9655 for the Pw marginal sweep, 0.9006 for the joint fit, 0.8973 for combined marginals.
 - setup: QAT trade-off grid at D=13B tokens, N 30-100M+, integer type, forward pass only quantized. Weights, activations and KV effects are independent and multiplicative (Finding 2). Table 1 compares forms: Neff has val R2 0.82 with 3 parameters.
 - quote: "the gains from increasing the bit precision of the weights are large at lower precisions but saturate at higher precisions (typically around 6-7 bits per weight)."
 - where: Sec 4.1-4.2, Eq 3-4, App K and C.
 - Activations and KV are more sensitive than weights: runs with Pa ≤ 3 or Pkv ≤ 3 "are not numerically stable, and often diverge, while Pw = 3 is still well behaved" (App L). They note this may be because activations are quantized per-tensor and weights per-channel.

6. Unified law (Finding 4): L = A·Neff^(−α) + B·D^(−β) + E + δPTQ(N,D,Pw,Pa,Pkv,Ppost).
 - number: δPTQ = C_T e^(−Ppost/γpost) (D^γD / Neff^γN) ∏_{x∈{w,a,kv}} [1−e^(−Cx(Px−Ppost))]. R2 = 0.90 on over 1000 data points from 465 pretraining runs, each PTQ'd to several precisions.
 - quote: "models trained in lower precision are more robust to post-train quantization in the sense of incurring lower degradation."
 - where: Sec 5, Eq 8-11, p.10-12.
 - Two competing effects. Robustification (training with noise) wins over the overtraining effect from smaller Neff. Degradation is defined as zero when Ptrain = Ppost.

7. Scale of experiments, and an internal inconsistency to note.
 - number: 465 pretraining runs at 3-16 bits. The abstract says validation on "up to 1.7B parameters trained on up to 26B tokens".
 - Sec 2.3 says the fitting sweep is N 30-220M and D up to 26B, with over 20 runs per (N,D). The 1.7B scale appears only in Fig 1 right (FP4 1.76B, FP6 1.17B, FP8 880M, BF16 440M, FP32 220M, N·P kept constant, all 16B tokens, floating point, "details in Appendix J"). Fig 6 text says "220M to 1.6B".
 - Fig 1 right final val losses: 3.233, 2.997, 3.009, 3.057, 3.198, in the order the labels are extracted. The extraction does not clearly map each loss to a precision, so verify against the figure.
 - where: abstract, Sec 2.3, Fig 1, App J.

8. Hyperparameters and Llama-3 context.
 - Llama-3-8B has D/N ≈ 2000 and Gemma-2 above 1000 (quoted from the paper's background). Laws are analysed to D/N ≈ 10^5.
 - Hyperparameters: seq len 1024, batch 256, peak LR 6e-4 (smallest model), depth-µP, weight decay 0.1, Adam β (0.9, 0.95). Ablation on C4 shows the same trends.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: fixed vanilla architecture (low-precision training often uses tweaks that "close much of the gap"). Gains from halving precision are usually under 2x. Loss only, no downstream evals. Trends are "suggestive rather than prescriptive".
- Fitted constants "unlikely to be useful"; the trends are the contribution.
- Small models (≤220M for fitting). Larger ones are only for the Fig 1 and Fig 6 checks.
- Laws are fitted on integer type, with only the forward pass quantized. Floating point is a hint (App N: γw=2.8111, 140 runs, R2 0.9678). The paper says the match "suggests that similar scaling laws may exist across types".
- PTQ is weights only (GPTQ, with AWQ and RTN replications). KV-cache or activation PTQ is not studied.
- Per-tensor vs per-channel granularity ablation in App I.
- App H explanations (sharpness, hierarchical learning) are marked "speculative".
- Fit quality is not uniform: R2 0.90 for the unified law, and outliers at extreme low precision are unstable.
- Dated: 2024, FP8 era. FP4 hardware is only described as "next generation".

BUILDS ON: Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla, L = A·N^−α + B·D^−β + E, D/N ≈ 20); Kaplan et al. 2020; Muennighoff et al. 2024b (tied α=β, held-out fit method); Sardana and Frankle 2023 and Gadre et al. 2024 (overtraining); Dettmers and Zettlemoyer 2023 (k-bit inference scaling, total model bits); Allen-Zhu and Li 2024; GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2022); AWQ (Lin et al. 2023); Micikevicius et al. 2022 (FP8); Ma et al. 2024 and Wang et al. 2023 (BitNet / 1.58-bit); Abdelkhalik et al. 2022 (compute linear in precision).

CODE: none. Key equations are above. Eq 7 gives the implicit P*(C). Cost model: C = (6/16)·N·D·P.

FIGURES (captions)
- Fig 1, p.2: left, PTQ degradation vs token/parameter ratio, "more pretraining compute worse at inference time"; right, larger models trained at lower precision at matched compute. Best single summary.
- Fig 2, p.5: PTQ loss and degradation vs D/N for 30M to 220M, INT3-6, fit R2 = 0.97.
- Fig 3: Neff/N vs bits, and empirical vs predicted iso-loss contours (D=13B).
- Fig 6: predicted vs empirical compute-optimal precision for INT and FP, plus P*(D) curves.
- Fig 7: unified PTQ fit heatmaps, training vs post-train precision.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean text, but figure data is garbled axis numbers. Table 2 labels the activation constant "γi" and "ni", and the text calls it γa. Several exponent and fraction equations were flattened (Eq 6, 16-17), so I took the forms from Eq 6 as printed. The abstract's "1.7B" claim does not match the Sec 2.3 sweep range (see claim 7). No prompt-injection text found.
